body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students follow a multistep procedure to extract DNA and explain the purpose of each step (RST.9-10.3).
- Students use the symbols and terms of molecular genetics (base pairs, codon, anticodon, mRNA, amino acid) to transcribe and translate genes and to predict the effect of mutations (RST.9-10.4).
- Students analyze the relationships among DNA, RNA, protein and trait, and the structure of the genetic code (RST.9-10.5).
- Students write an informative explanation of how a single mutation causes sickle cell disease, citing specific evidence from a text (WHST.9-10.2, RST.9-10.1).

MATERIALS
- DNA extraction, per group: 2 or 3 fresh or thawed strawberries, a zip-top bag, extraction buffer (100 mL water, 10 mL dish soap, 1.5 g salt, about 1/4 teaspoon), a coffee filter and funnel, a clear test tube or narrow cup, ice-cold 91% isopropyl or 95% ethanol alcohol (kept in a freezer), a wooden stick or paper clip hook
- A DNA model or paper base-pair cut-outs
- The Genetic Code (Selected Codons) handout, provided as a reading in the activities
- Goggles; keep alcohol away from any flame

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read From Code to Character. Build a short DNA model with paper bases and have students discover the pairing rule. Show how unzipping and rebuilding produces two identical molecules (semiconservative replication). Connect back: an allele is a sequence.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Strawberry DNA Extraction. Before starting, groups predict what each ingredient does. After, they explain why we can see DNA when a single molecule is far too thin to see (millions of strands clump together).
Day 3: Transcription and translation. Act it out: one student is the DNA in the nucleus, another carries the mRNA message to the ribosome, and tRNA cards bring amino acids. Practice decoding with the codon table. Start Transcription and Translation Practice.
Day 4: Mutations: substitution (silent, missense, nonsense) and insertion or deletion (frameshift). Read Sickle Cell: One Letter, Many Lives. Students plan the informative essay From One Letter to a Disease with a level-by-level organizer (DNA, mRNA, protein, cell, body, population).
Day 5: Assessment: DNA and Proteins Check (one class period, no AI help; students may use the codon table).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a step chart (DNA template, mRNA, codons split by slashes, amino acids) and have students split every sequence into triplets before decoding. Color-code the bases.
- Support: for the essay, give the six-level organizer with the first sentence of each paragraph started.
- Extension: research how CRISPR-based gene therapy for sickle cell disease works, and explain why it targets blood stem cells rather than mature red blood cells (which have no nucleus).
- Extension: explain why the genetic code is called redundant, and why redundancy makes some substitutions harmless.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): many terms are cognates (ADN, ARN, proteina, aminoacido, mutacion, transcripcion, traduccion). Point out that transcription and translation mean what they mean in language: copying in the same language (DNA and RNA both use bases) and translating into a new one (bases into amino acids). Accept oral explanations of the extraction steps with a labeled photo sequence.
- Safety: alcohol is flammable and should stay cold and capped; wear goggles.

FAMILY NOTE
This week your student extracted real DNA from strawberries using dish soap, salt and alcohol, and is learning how the DNA code is read to build proteins. We are using sickle cell disease as an example of how a change in a single letter of DNA can change a protein and a person's health. If your student wants to try the extraction at home, all it takes is a strawberry, a sealable bag, a little dish soap, salt, water and rubbing alcohol from the freezer, with an adult nearby.

Note for teachers: some students may have sickle cell disease or trait, or family members who do. Present it as science and medicine, not as a story about any group, and avoid asking students to share their own health information.
title: Teacher guide: DNA and Proteins
